title: The summit
hookLine: five years of mornings: a carpenter's son, a book, a long story, many rooms, a life; the hill goes on, and so do you
tomorrow: the hill goes on. where will you start again tomorrow morning?

cards: On a hike, the climb is all breath and feet and the next rock. Then the top, and you turn around: the whole valley at once, roads and towns and people you couldn't see on the way up.
Five years of mornings are down there too. A carpenter's son from Nazareth. A book, read page by page.
A long story. A house with many rooms. A life to live it in.

teach.h: THE HILL IS WHERE YOU LOOK UP.
teach.b: So what is a summit for? A psalm answers, in the King James: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." The help isn't the hill.
The hill is where you look up from. In Mark, Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain and is transfigured before them.

teach.h: GOOD TO BE HERE, THEN DOWN.
teach.b: Peter says, "Master, it is good for us to be here," and offers to build shelters so they can stay. The story doesn't stay. A cloud, a voice, and they come down, to a crowd, an argument, and a father with a sick son.
A summit is for seeing clearly, then going back down to people. And from up here you can see how many people there are.
Paul, speaking in Athens, says God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Muslims have a verse that sounds close.

The Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." One family, made different so they'd know one another.

That's real shared ground. The difference is real too: Paul's speech goes on to Jesus raised from the dead, and Muslims understand Jesus differently. Neither has to pretend otherwise to look out on the same valley.
The psalm ends past the top: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Not a finish line.

how: Churches remember the transfiguration on the mountain in the church year, and some Christians read or sing Psalm 121 before a journey or a parting.

o: a prize at the top for those who finished first
the end of the road, where the walking stops
the top of the hill: look back, give thanks, go on

games.q: you're Peter on the mountain. it's good to be here, and you offer to build shelters and stay. what happens next in Mark?
o: they stay up there for days.
a cloud, a voice, and they come down to a waiting crowd.
games.why: Mark 9:7–17: the cloud, the voice, the coming down, and at the bottom a crowd, scribes questioning, and a father with his son. the summit is for seeing, then going back to people.

practice: Stand, if you can, and be still. Look out at whatever is in front of you, a window, a wall, a patch of sky, and let five years of mornings come back: a face, a line, a day that stayed. Then give thanks for one of them, out loud.

wordCard.voice: The summit. A place to stand still and look back, and then, like Peter, James and John, to come down again among people.

orig.note: Greek: he was transfigured, changed in form, in Mark 9:2.

carryVoice: Your line: start again, from here. The hill goes on, and so do you, wherever the road leads next.
